item.title: MCP is changing the questions marketers can afford to ask
item.description:
Picture a regional marketing director on a Monday morning. She’s got 80 locations, a cup of coffee, and a nagging feeling that something is off in the Southeast. Reviews seem quieter. A couple of stores got new managers last month. Are those two things related?

Not long ago, finding out meant pulling an export, building a pivot table, pulling a second export from another system, and stitching it all together in a spreadsheet. Or, more realistically, filing a request with an analyst and waiting. Most weeks, the question simply never got asked.

Now she types it into the AI assistant her company already rolled out, and it answers using live data from the systems where that data actually lives.

The technology making that possible is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP. You’ve probably read plenty of “what is MCP” explainers by now, so I won’t add another. Instead, I want to talk about what changes for marketing teams, especially those managing lots of locations, when a cross-system question gets this cheap to ask. And what CIOs need to get right before it becomes the normal way marketing works.

The real shift: the join moves into the conversation

Here’s the short version of how MCP works. Your AI assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini, or something your team built) is the host. Each business system, like your reputation platform, ad account, or CRM, publishes an MCP server. That server tells the assistant, in plain language, what it can do: “I can summarize reviews for a group of locations,” or “I can check whether your listings match across Google and Apple Maps.” The assistant reads that menu, picks the right tools for the question, and calls them.

That’s really it. But two things fall out of it that matter a lot for marketing.

First, the integration math gets much friendlier. Connecting four assistants to ten marketing systems used to mean up to 40 custom integrations. With a shared protocol, each assistant learns MCP once, and each system publishes one server. The conversation shifts from “should we build this integration?” to “which servers do we approve?”

Second, and this is the one people underestimate, the join moves. In a traditional stack, combining review data with POS and CRM data happens in a warehouse, on a schedule, through a pipeline someone has to own. With MCP, a regional leader can connect three systems to the same assistant and ask one question across all of them. The model does the join on the spot, right in the conversation, using that person’s own permissions.

That doesn’t replace your data warehouse. What it does is make a long tail of one-off, “I just want to know” questions affordable for the first time. In multi-location marketing, that long tail is where a lot of the useful insight lives.

It’s also not a science project anymore. Anthropic donated MCP to the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation last December, with OpenAI, Google, Microsoft, and AWS all involved. And the July 2026 spec update made it far more enterprise friendly. It now scales on ordinary infrastructure, lets IT control which tools can run at the gateway, and gives tools a standard way to stop and ask a human, “Are you sure?” before doing anything.

Location marketing is the ultimate stress test

If MCP works for brick-and-mortar marketing, it’ll work almost anywhere. Do the math on a mid-sized brand. Three hundred locations, each listed on Google, Apple Maps, Bing, and Yelp, add up to 1,200 profiles that all need the same name, address, phone number, and hours. Every location collects reviews every week on multiple sites. And each one sits inside a hierarchy of district, region, brand, and maybe franchisee, where every level is supposed to see a different slice.

On top of that, the questions people ask are almost always comparative. Nobody asks, “What’s store 114’s rating?” They ask, “Which stores in the Southeast are slipping, and why?” Those are exactly the questions dashboards handle badly, and exports handle slowly.

My colleague Kristi Melani recently wrote here about how reputation data is now moving in two directions: outward to the AI engines customers use, and inward to the assistants your own teams use. MCP is the plumbing for that inward direction, and it raises the stakes on data quality on both sides. A wrong Sunday hour on Apple Maps used to mislead one customer. Now it can mislead that customer’s AI and your CMO’s AI at the same time. Customers already punish that mistake: Rio SEO found that 53% of consumers are unlikely to visit a business with incorrect listings.

What this actually looks like

The pattern I’m seeing in multi-location brands is pretty consistent. MCP doesn’t replace the reputation platform, the listings tool, or the ad account. It changes who gets to ask them questions, how often, and in what combinations. A few examples:

  • The field leader asks, “Which of my locations collected zero reviews this month, and what happened to their scores?” That used to be a weekly export, filtered by hand.
  • The local search lead asks, “Where do our hours or phone numbers disagree across Google, Apple Maps, Bing, and Yelp badly enough that an AI assistant would get them wrong?” That used to be a quarterly audit.
  • The paid media lead asks, “Which markets are we spending the most in where our average rating dropped below 4.0?” Google already publishes an official Google Ads MCP server, so that’s now one question instead of two dashboards and a spreadsheet.
  • The CMO asks for the first-half reputation readout by market, with the three biggest opportunities. That used to be two or three days of deck-building.

The industry-specific versions get even more interesting. A dealer group can read service department reviews next to repair order data. A property manager can line up resident complaints with open maintenance tickets, building by building. A restaurant brand can check whether a spike in “cold food” reviews lines up with a change in delivery partners. None of that needed new infrastructure. It just needed both systems to have a server, and the person asking to have access to both.

Tool design matters more than tool count

Here’s something that surprises a lot of teams once they start piloting: the shape of the tools matters more than how many there are.

An AI assistant works within a limited context window and a limited number of tool calls. If a regional director asks about 300 locations and the server only offers a one-location-at-a-time lookup, the model has to make 300 calls and juggle 300 results. It’ll be slow, it’ll be expensive, or it’ll quietly skip some. A server that can roll up an entire region in one call hands the model a small, tidy result it can actually reason about.

The same goes for definitions. If “sentiment” is calculated differently on every review site, the model will happily compare numbers that aren’t comparable. MCP can’t fix that, because it just moves data. Consistent metrics have to exist before the assistant ever sees them.

So when you evaluate a marketing MCP server, don’t ask how many tools it has. Ask whether it can answer a portfolio-level question in one or two calls, using metrics that mean the same thing everywhere.

Connecting is easy. Governing is the real work.

Hooking an assistant up to a marketing system now takes minutes. Deciding whether you should is where CIOs and AI governance teams are spending their time. Four questions come up in nearly every conversation I have.

Whose permissions does the assistant use? The safest setup is for each person to sign in as themselves, so the assistant inherits their existing access. A district manager who sees 12 locations in the platform should see 12 through the assistant, not 300. What you want to avoid is a shared API key baked into a connector, which quietly gives everyone the widest access anyone has.

Can it change anything? Reading a review summary and posting a public reply to a customer are very different levels of risk. Review responses and listing fixes are where AI promises the biggest time savings, but they’re also public and attached to your brand. Plenty of organizations are starting read-only and adding write access one tool at a time, with a human approving each action.

What is the assistant actually reading? This one is specific to reputation data, and it doesn’t get talked about enough. Reviews are written by the public. A review can include text aimed at an AI rather than a person, essentially an instruction hiding in plain sight. If the same conversation also has tools that can send email or edit records, that’s a real risk. Keeping reputation access read-only, and keeping anything that publishes behind a confirmation step, shrinks that exposure a lot.

Where does the data go? Review text can contain names, health details, and other personal information. In healthcare, a review can effectively confirm that someone is a patient. Governance teams need to know which AI tools are approved for which kinds of data, and what each AI vendor’s enterprise agreement says about retention and training.

Underneath all four is a simpler truth: MCP makes your data easier to reach. It doesn’t make it more accurate. Gartner predicts that through 2026, organizations will abandon 60% of AI projects that lack AI-ready data. For local marketing, “AI-ready” means one location list every system agrees on, consistent metrics, and listings that are actually correct. If your store IDs don’t match between the reputation platform, the POS, and the CRM, the assistant’s answers will break in exactly the spots an analyst used to patch by hand.

Where to start

The organizations moving fastest treat MCP as a joint project between IT and marketing, not a feature marketing flips on by itself. Here’s the path I’d recommend:

  1. Start with the questions, not the systems. Ask your regional leaders for the ten questions they ask most and wait longest to get answered. That tells you which servers actually matter.
  2. Go read-only, per user, in one region. Approve a small set of servers that inherit existing permissions, and pilot with a team that’s already using an enterprise AI assistant.
  3. Clean up your location list before you scale. It’s unglamorous work. It’s also what decides whether cross-system answers are right.
  4. Add write access slowly, with a human in the loop. Review responses and listing corrections is the obvious next step. Set your brand voice and compliance rules before the first reply goes out.

Whatever servers you evaluate, make sure they work across every major assistant. An open standard is what saves you from rebuilding everything the next time your company switches AI vendors.

From questions to agents

Right now, most marketing use of MCP is a person asking a question. The next phase is software asking on a schedule: an agent that checks every location each morning, flags a listing that’s drifted, or drafts replies to overnight reviews for a manager to approve. Those agents will run on the same servers answering human questions today.

It’s already happening in other parts of the business. When the latest MCP spec was announced, Honeycomb shared that nearly 20% of its monthly interactive queries now come from agents, not people. Marketing data won’t be far behind.

That’s why the choices made in this first wave matter so much. When we built the Reputation MCP Server, we made it read-only and permission-based from day one, because an agent is only as trustworthy as the data it can reach and the access it’s allowed.

The protocol is open to everyone. What will set brands apart is the quality of the data they plug into it and how carefully they govern it. For marketers responsible for hundreds of storefronts, the questions that used to wait for the quarterly review are about to get asked every Monday morning. The brands that get their data ready will see their locations more clearly than ever.

item.title: Human in the loop is an engineering problem
item.description:
A customer leaves a one-star review at one of your locations. An AI drafts a reply in seconds. It’s warm, on-brand, grammatically perfect, and it thanks the customer for their feedback and invites them back soon.

The review was about a customer who slipped and was hurt in the parking lot.

Nothing in that reply is factually false. It would pass a spell-checker, a brand-voice check, and probably a quick skim from a busy manager. It’s still the wrong answer, and if it goes out publicly, it’s the kind of wrong that ends up in a screenshot.

I spend most of my time building systems that put AI to work on reputation data: reviews, listings, surveys, and the replies and summaries generated from them. The most important lesson I’ve learned is that “human in the loop” is an engineering problem. Where the human sits, what they see, what gets routed to them and what doesn’t—all of that is system design.

Get it right, and AI can move fast without embarrassing you. Get it wrong, and you either drown your reviewers or give them a rubber stamp.

What “human in the loop” means

The phrase gets used loosely, so let’s pin it down. From a systems perspective, there are three oversight modes:

  • Human in the loop is a synchronous approval gate. The AI proposes, a person approves, and nothing happens until they do.
  • Human on the loop is asynchronous monitoring. The AI acts on its own, while people watch dashboards, review samples, and get alerts, and they can step in or shut it off.
  • Human out of the loop is full automation. Guardrails and logging only, no person in the path.

The mistake I see most often is choosing one mode for an entire product. Choose it per action instead. Pulling a summary of last month’s reviews and publishing a reply to a customer can live in the same application, but they carry completely different risk profiles and shouldn’t share an oversight mode. A good system might run a dozen actions out of the loop, a handful on the loop, and gate one or two behind a person.

Regulators are writing the same principle into law. The EU AI Act’s Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed so people can effectively oversee them, with oversight “commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use,” and it specifically calls out the danger of people over-relying on AI output. Most marketing uses won’t fall into the Act’s high-risk categories, but Article 14 shows where expectations are heading.

The U.S. military’s directive on autonomy in weapon systems has asked for “appropriate levels of human judgment over the use of force” since 2012. That means the appropriate level of judgment for the stakes rather than a human on every decision, which is the same principle at far higher stakes.

Accurate isn’t the same as right

Large language models generate the most plausible next words, and they don’t look facts up unless you build the LLMs to persistently fact-check or cite claims. When plausible and true diverge, you get a hallucination, a confident, fluent answer that’s made up. The fluency is the dangerous part, because it reads exactly like a correct answer.

When we test AI output, we check for two kinds of accuracy.

Factual accuracy asks whether a statement is true. Did a location page list a service that location doesn’t offer? These errors are easier to catch, because you can compare them against a source of truth.

Contextual accuracy asks whether it’s true here, now, for this person. These errors are sneakier, because every individual fact can check out:

  • The holiday hours are correct, but they’re the hours for a different region.
  • A sentiment model scores “great, another two-hour wait” as positive, because it reads the word “great” and misses the sarcasm.
  • And our injury review reply from the top of this piece: right tone for 95% of reviews, wrong for this one.

Not every error carries the same weight, and your system should know the difference. I think about it in three tiers:

  • Embarrassing: a fabricated statistic in a published report, or an off-key public reply. Painful, fixable, and memorable for the wrong reasons.
  • Foundational: an error early in a project that everything else gets built on, like a quarter’s worth of misclassified review themes feeding a campaign strategy that’s wrong from the start.
  • Dangerous: errors that can hurt people. In marketing, that’s a healthcare review reply that confirms someone is a patient, or wrong pharmacy hours during a storm. Outside marketing, it’s AI in public safety, healthcare, infrastructure, and defense, where “mostly right” is not an acceptable standard and human judgment isn’t optional.

The tiers matter because they decide where the human goes. You can’t afford a person on every output, and you can’t afford no person on the dangerous ones.

Anatomy of a human-in-the-loop pipeline

When we design an oversight system, it looks less like “a person checks the AI” and more like a pipeline, where each layer catches what it’s best at and passes the rest along. Here’s the shape of it.

Reputation

Most drafts never need a person. The ones that do arrive with the evidence a reviewer needs, and every human decision feeds back into the system.

1. Grounding. The first defense against hallucination is not letting the model work from memory. We connect it to authoritative sources, like the location master record and approved policies, and require every factual claim to point back to one.

2. Deterministic validators. Cheap, fast, boring checks run next. Do the hours match the system of record? Does the reply contain a banned phrase, a competitor’s name, or personal information it shouldn’t? Software should catch everything software can catch.

3. Model-based verifiers. A second model checks whether each claim is supported by its source and whether the tone fits the review. It catches contextual errors that rules can’t, like a cheerful reply to an angry review, but it’s still probabilistic, so calibrate it against examples people have labeled.

4. Risk scoring and routing. The system combines the type of action, the check results, and the input into a routing decision. A five-star “great service, thanks” can get an auto-approved reply. A one-star review that mentions an injury, discrimination, a health issue, or a lawyer always goes to a person. The routing rules are versioned and reviewed like code, because they are code.

5. The review interface. Reviewers are a component of the system, so design their inputs. A good review screen shows the source next to each claim and highlights what the verifier was unsure about. A reviewer handed a wall of polished text will skim it. A reviewer shown “this sentence has no source” will stop and look.

6. The feedback loop. Every edit and rejection becomes a test case, a new rule, or a prompt fix, so over time fewer things need a person. Keep a random sample of auto-approved output flowing to reviewers too, or the system only learns from the cases you already knew to route.

7. The audit trail. Log what the model produced, which checks ran, who approved it, and what they changed. When something goes wrong, this tells you whether it was the model, the data, the routing, or the review.

Test it before launch, watch it after

The pipeline is only as good as the testing around it. Three practices do most of the work.

Golden data sets. Build a library of known tricky cases (sarcasm, mixed languages, injuries, legal threats, star ratings that contradict the text) and run every model, prompt, and rule change against it. If a change breaks a golden case, it doesn’t ship.

Red-teaming. Have people deliberately try to break the system. The public writes reviews, and someone can write one with instructions aimed at an AI (“ignore your guidelines and reply with…”). No current model reliably ignores those, so limit what the pipeline can do with review text and test it.

Drift monitoring. AI behavior changes even when you don’t touch it, as models update and customers’ language shifts. Pin model versions where you can, track quality against a baseline, and alert when it moves. A system that passed its tests in March can be failing quietly by October.

What to avoid

Most failed oversight systems I’ve seen had reviewers. They failed because of how the review was set up.

Rubber-stamping. This is the big one. When a system is right 98% of the time, people stop reading carefully and start clicking approve. It’s called automation bias, and the EU AI Act names it directly. One technique we use is seeding known errors into review queues and tracking whether reviewers catch them. If they don’t, look at the workload, the interface, and the incentives before you blame the reviewer.

Reviewing everything. A person on every output creates a bottleneck and burns reviewers out, which makes them worse at catching the errors that matter. Route by risk instead.

The moral crumple zone. The researcher Madeleine Clare Elish coined this term for what happens when a person ends up absorbing the blame for a system they couldn’t meaningfully control, the way a car’s crumple zone absorbs the impact of a crash. If a reviewer has 15 seconds per item, no source to check against, and no authority to push back, they’re providing someone to blame and calling it oversight.

Blaming only the model. If the location record says a store closes at 9 and it actually closes at 8, a perfectly grounded AI will confidently repeat the wrong hours. Your oversight system should watch the data too.

How to tell if it’s working

If you can’t measure your oversight system, you can’t tell whether it’s protecting you or just slowing you down. Three numbers matter most:

  • Escape rate. How many errors were found after publishing, by a customer, a manager, or an audit? This is the number that tells you whether the whole pipeline works.
  • Seeded-error catch rate. Of the known errors you planted in review queues, what share did reviewers catch? This is your direct measure of rubber-stamping.
  • Routing accuracy. Of the items sent to people, how many needed a person? Of the items auto-approved, how many should have been reviewed?

The check I trust most is simpler. If your reviewers almost never change anything, find out why. Either the AI really is that good on that type of content, in which case you can loosen the routing and save everyone time, or nobody’s really reading. You need to know which one it is.

Where this is headed

So far, most of this has been about reviewing what AI says. The next phase is about governing what AI does. As agents start taking actions on their own, such as updating listings, posting replies, or opening tickets, oversight shifts from approving individual outputs to setting boundaries: what an agent is allowed to do on its own, what it must stop and ask about, and what it can never do.

The standards are starting to build this in. The Model Context Protocol specification, the open standard many AI assistants now use to connect to business systems, says there should always be a human in the loop who can deny a tool call, and recommends that apps ask the user to confirm sensitive operations. Where that gate sits is still each app’s design decision.

The human role is changing too. Less proofreading of every output, more supervising: writing the routing rules, handling the exceptions the system escalates, auditing samples, and deciding where the boundaries should sit. At Reputation, that’s how we think about the people in our loops. Their job is to teach the system what “right” looks like.

As models get better, the errors that slip through get rarer and subtler, which makes them harder to spot. A system that’s wrong 10% of the time keeps everyone alert. A system that’s wrong 0.5% of the time lulls people into trusting it, and that’s when a well-designed loop matters most.

For more information, visit reputation.com.

About the author

Thomas Medina is the Director of AI at Reputation. He is an engineering leader focused on building complex AI systems and scalable human-in-the-loop architectures. He brings a deep engineering tenure at Reputation specializing in designing automated verification pipelines, safety guardrails, and governance frameworks for autonomous AI systems.

item.title: Beyond the perimeter: The network as the security fabric for the AI era
item.description:
Enterprises have historically built separate network and security architectures, but this separation is becoming increasingly difficult to maintain as frontier AI models mature and security architectures shift from perimeter-based defenses to identity- and context-aware enforcement.

Frontier AI does not change existing cybersecurity fundamentals; it narrows the time available to apply them. As attacks move from human speed to machine speed, enterprises need security controls that can detect, respond, and enforce at the same speed. The network is uniquely positioned to become that enforcement and containment fabric.

The AI era requires enterprises to treat the network as an active security control, not simply as infrastructure to be protected. By integrating identity, telemetry, segmentation, and automated enforcement, the network can reduce exposure, contain compromise, and accelerate recovery at machine speed.

A brief look at how security has evolved

Traditional firewalls established an enterprise perimeter, while demilitarized zones created controlled, externally facing segments that restricted access to internal resources. Network access control lists added another enforcement layer by limiting communication to or from IP addresses associated with unauthorized users and devices.

As threats evolved, enterprises needed controls more granular than zones and IP addresses. Architectures such as Cisco ACI and TrustSec enabled application traffic to be permitted or denied according to identity and context, rather than relying only on addressing or device type.

Next-generation firewalls extended this identity- and context-aware model to perimeter enforcement by distinguishing among applications, users, devices, content, and threats.

The migration of workloads, applications, and data to cloud environments expanded the security boundary beyond enterprise-controlled infrastructure and required controls designed for cloud configuration, workloads, applications, and access.

Software-defined WAN then helped establish the Secure Access Service Edge model, combining SD-WAN connectivity with Security Service Edge capabilities such as secure web gateways, cloud access security brokers, firewall as a service, and zero-trust network access.

The frontier AI era

Frontier models have crossed an important cybersecurity threshold: AI-based models can increasingly discover vulnerabilities, develop exploits, orchestrate attack chains, and operate with levels of autonomy that compress attack cycles from days or hours to machine speed.

Enterprises must therefore now design security architectures on the assumption that compromise will occur.

This change demands a security strategy that reduces exposure before an attack, contains damage during a breach, accelerates response, and restores operations quickly.

The key pillars of this security approach are:

  • Attack surface management: Reducing exploitable opportunities and weaknesses.
  • Blast radius reduction: Reducing the scope of damage when a breach occurs.
  • AI-enhanced security operations: Accelerating detection and response so defenders can keep pace with machine-speed attacks.
  • Enhanced resilience and recovery: Restoring critical services rapidly and reducing the overall impact on the enterprise.

Supporting measures will include stronger patch management, segmentation as a core cyber-resilience capability, and virtual shielding. Together, these controls minimize the attack surface and reduce the blast radius where vulnerabilities cannot be remediated immediately.

Identity governance must extend beyond human users to include non-human identities associated with agentic AI, automated systems, and the internet of things. Unlike traditional users, who typically interact with applications and systems one action at a time, AI agents can operate continuously, interact directly with APIs, and other agents, and execute actions at machine speed.

Zero trust is evolving from an access architecture into a continuous operating model in which every request to a protected resource is explicitly authenticated and authorized, regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the enterprise environment.

In a zero-trust environment, identity determines which resources a user, device, workload, or agent may access. The network then becomes a critical control point for limiting how far that authorized access can extend across the enterprise.

The network as the enforcement fabric

Enterprises should prioritize their most critical business services, automate security operations, and strengthen network resilience so that prevention, containment, response, and recovery function as one operating model. Within that model, the secure network must provide five core capabilities:

  • Visibility: Provides visibility into traffic between users, devices, workloads, applications, APIs, agents, and data.
  • Enforcement: Convert identity, posture, application, and threat intelligence into access decisions.
  • Segmentation: Prevent a compromised identity, workload, or AI agent from becoming an enterprise-wide compromise.
  • Telemetry: Use network behavior as a detection signal for increasingly rapid and autonomous attacks.
  • Containment: Isolate workloads, revoke communication paths, and constrain east-west movement at machine speed.

In the frontier AI era, preventing every breach is no longer a realistic strategy. The objective is to make compromise difficult, lateral movement constrained, detection immediate, and recovery rapid. Achieving that objective requires identity, endpoint, cloud, and application security to operate as an integrated system, with the network providing the visibility, segmentation, and enforcement fabric that connects them.

The network is no longer simply infrastructure to be secured. It is becoming part of the security architecture itself.

Hear from the experts

How can enterprises turn the network into an active layer of security in the AI era? Watch this webinar to hear experts from NTT DATA, Cisco, and IDC discuss how organizations can evolve their network architectures to improve visibility, contain threats, and strengthen resilience.

item.title: Don’t start with AI. Start with the work
item.description:
There is a lot of discussion about deploying AI across the enterprise. Most of it starts with the model, the platform or the tool. I start somewhere else: the work.

What decision are we trying to improve? What information does a person need at that moment? What gets in the way today? And what should the technology do when the situation does not fit the standard process? Those questions matter whether the employee is working at a desk, supporting a customer, writing software or managing a shift.

The work is different across those environments, but the technology challenge is connected. AI creates value when it is grounded in the context of the work and built into the workflow. It does not create value simply because it has been deployed.

That distinction is important for CIOs. At UKG, our own employees are primarily desk-based. My responsibility is not to run frontline operations. But we build technology for organizations whose work includes both corporate and frontline employees, so we have to understand both environments. The CIO’s role is to create the architecture, standards and operating model that allow AI to be useful across them.

Start with the outcome

The first question should not be, “Where can we add AI?” It should be, “Where would better information or faster execution change the outcome?”

For a desk-based team, that might mean reducing the time required to find the answer to a customer question, helping an engineer understand a complex codebase or giving a finance leader a clearer view of a business trend. For a frontline manager, it might mean identifying a staffing risk before a shift begins or helping resolve an exception without moving between several systems.

The use cases are different, but the method is the same. Map the workflow end to end. Identify the decisions, handoffs, systems and exceptions. Then decide what should be automated, what should be augmented and what should remain a human decision. If the process does not change, AI often becomes another layer on top of the existing friction.

Build the context layer

AI is not plug and play. A model can generate an answer, but a reliable answer depends on the context behind it: the right data, the user’s role and permissions, the current operating state, relevant history and the policies that govern the decision.

That context looks different depending on the work. An employee in an office may need project, customer, financial or technical information. A frontline employee may need current staffing, scheduling, compliance or operational information. In both cases, disconnected data creates the same problem: The system may be able to produce a response, but not necessarily one that is relevant, trusted or actionable.

This is why I think of the context layer as an architectural priority. CIOs need clear systems of record, reliable data, appropriate access controls and a defined way to retrieve and validate information. They also need to understand the difference between an answer, a recommendation and an action. Those are not interchangeable.

Redesign the work, not just the interface

There is a productivity gap that shows up in many AI programs. An organization deploys a tool, people use it and leaders expect the return to appear. But the work, roles and decision rights have not changed. That is not transformation. It is an additional tool.

If an AI system identifies a risk, who is responsible for acting on it? Can the person closest to the work resolve it? What constraints apply? When does the issue require escalation? A useful AI experience has to answer those questions as part of the workflow.

That requires close partnership among IT, business leaders, HR and the people doing the work. The technology team can provide the platform, integration and controls, but the business owns the outcome. The design also has to reflect how people actually work: different devices, different levels of access, different amounts of time and different levels of technical comfort.

Design with people, not for them

The people closest to the work are an important source of context. That includes an analyst who knows where a reporting process breaks, a customer-support employee who sees recurring issues or a frontline manager who understands what a staffing recommendation would mean in practice.

Representative employees should be involved in mapping, testing and improving the workflow. They should have a clear way to identify an incorrect answer, challenge a recommendation and report when a new process creates unintended work. That feedback is not a change-management afterthought. It is part of building a reliable system.

The CIO also has to be clear about the role of AI. The objective is not to remove human judgment from every process. It is to use technology where it improves speed, consistency and decision quality, while keeping people accountable for the decisions that require expertise, empathy or judgment.

Make the “3 Ts” decision

When we look at an AI use case, I find it useful to make what I call the “3 Ts” decision. Does the work require Talent for judgment or expertise? Can existing Tools solve it efficiently? Or do Tokens create enough value to justify the investment?

The answer will vary by workflow. A high-volume task may be a strong candidate for automation. A complex decision may need AI to surface the relevant information while a person remains accountable. In some cases, the best answer is not another model; it is a simpler process or a better integration.

This is also where CIOs need discipline around measurement. Prompts, licenses, logins and interactions are signals of activity. They are not proof of value. Measure whether the work is better: whether decisions are stronger, cycle times are shorter, errors are reduced, customers are better served or employees can spend more time on high-value work. Then pair those measures with trust and experience signals.

The CIO agenda

If I were evaluating an AI opportunity today, I would ask these questions:

  • What business outcome are we trying to improve?
  • What context does the workflow require and can we provide it reliably and securely?
  • What needs to change in the process, role or decision rights?
  • Have we designed with the people who will use the system and the people affected by its decisions?
  • How will we know the work is better, rather than simply knowing that the tool is being used?

Enterprise AI will not be one experience for every employee. A desk-based employee and a frontline employee may need different interfaces, information and workflows. But they should be supported by the same underlying discipline: trusted context, clear accountability, human judgment and a focus on outcomes.

That is the work of the CIO. Simplify where we can. Standardize where it creates leverage. Scale what proves valuable. The goal is not to deploy more AI. The goal is to help people make better decisions and do better work — wherever that work happens.

item.title: How to move fast with AI and still maintain customer trust
item.description:
Companies are moving fast to put AI into chatbots, virtual assistants, and other customer service tools. But for CIOs, that comes with a risk: if the technology gives customers the wrong information, makes biased recommendations, or mishandles data, it can immediately damage the trust companies have worked hard to build.

Unlike conventional software, gen AI doesn’t always give the same answer to the same question. An answer can sound confident and convincing while still wrong. And when customers rely on AI for information about their finances, insurance, or health, a mistake can have much greater consequences.

Sumit Johar, CIO at cloud-based software company BlackLine, understands that inaccurate AI responses hurt the customer experience, force companies to spend money and resources to fix problems, damage the brand, and create regulatory risks. AI systems can also expose confidential information, making it important for companies to understand the data sources behind their responses.

“An AI failure creates a massive trust issue around the core solution being provided,” Johar says. “In the financial sector, bad AI advice or outputs can compromise balance sheet accuracy and lead to severe legal and personal liabilities.”

For Citizen Health CTO Daniel Wang, for instance, the stakes are particularly high because the company’s users include rare disease patients and caregivers.

Citizen Health works to ensure that important information provided by its AI can be traced back to the original source, such as patient records, clinical information, or medical studies. The company also reminds patients to talk with their healthcare providers before making medical decisions.

Wang says one of his biggest concerns isn’t just that AI can make a mistake, but that a wrong answer can sound right.

“An AI system can present an answer that sounds caring, informative, and authoritative, even when the underlying information is inaccurate,” he says.

That risk has affected how Citizen Health releases AI products, and has delayed AI launches when the company needed more time to understand how the technology was coming up with its answers, or to make sure those answers were accurate. So instead of rolling out new AI tools to everyone at once, smaller groups of patients might be tested first, and their feedback used to make improvements before a wider launch.

Citizen Health also tests its AI tools before launch using questions with known answers, and uses both automated testing and human review, watches for unusual AI responses, limits what the AI can answer, and gives patients ways to provide feedback.

Moving at the speed of trust

Other tech leaders are taking a similarly cautious approach. Jonathan Tushman, CTO and CAIO at Hi Marley, an insurance technology company, says it’s had tech that was ready to ship for years but chose to spend more time on testing, observability, legal review, and training before releasing it.

“If it weren’t for that trust-and-governance bar, we’d have gone live a year earlier and had faster adoption,” Tushman says. “We chose not to.”

Hi Marley calls that approach working at the speed of trust. For Tushman, releasing customer-facing AI also requires the ability to see what the system is doing once it’s running. That includes monitoring individual conversations as well as looking for patterns across tens of thousands of interactions. Companies also need kill switches that can shut down a system, and the ability to roll back changes if something goes wrong.

But technology alone isn’t enough. Customer service, IT, DevOps, and CloudOps teams all need procedures to respond to AI problems, Tushman adds.

Udaya Bhaskar, senior application security analyst at global farming company Corteva Agriscience, says one mistake companies make is moving too quickly after seeing an impressive AI demonstration without fully testing how the tech will perform with actual customers.

He adds that companies can also run into problems when they rely too heavily on vendor claims, or launch AI tools without giving customers an easy way to reach a person when something goes wrong.

The hidden cost of AI mistakes

The pressure to deploy AI is often tied to the promise of greater efficiency. A chatbot that handles more customer questions, for example, can reduce employee workloads. But those time and cost savings can shrink quickly if employees have to spend their time checking and correcting the AI, something referred to as the hallucination tax.

Companies may budget for developing the technology without fully accounting for ongoing costs of running and monitoring it.

Jess Lampe, global lead technologist at Launch Consulting says those hidden costs can include employees spending time checking AI responses and redoing work when the technology gets something wrong, as well as regulatory and legal risks. Another cost can be harder to measure: loss of customer trust.

Chris Slovak, global field CTO at managed enterprise AI delivery platform Unframe, sees the resulting damage to a company’s reputation as one of the largest hidden costs.

“Anything customer-facing is a representation of your brand,” Slovak says. “Yes, poor implementations with bad experiences have a material cost from the perspective of tokens. However, the impact on your brand is far more costly. Often, companies add AI to deflect customer support. Consider you have a customer who’s already frustrated, and meeting AI makes it worse. The loss in trust can be massive.”

But Kevan Yalowitz, global software and platforms lead at Accenture, says mistakes are going to happen whether work is performed by people or technology.

“The true hidden cost is destroying user trust when mistakes happen, regardless of the source,” Yalowitz says. “The most successful organizations quickly admit when these mistakes happen, provide a transparent explanation, and explain how it was an opportunity to learn and ensure the mistake doesn’t happen again.”

Human oversight remains critical

For CIOs, preventing those problems means putting controls around AI before it reaches customers.

Johar says human oversight is particularly important for critical decisions. In highly regulated industries such as finance, AI shouldn’t independently handle decisions where accuracy is essential. Companies also need reliable data feeding their AI systems, and the ability to audit what happens when something goes wrong.

Lampe says the level of oversight should depend on what an AI system is allowed to do. An AI tool that summarizes information, for example, doesn’t pose the same risk as one that can take action involving a customer’s money or account.

Companies should also continue testing after launch. AI behavior can change over time, meaning a system that performed well when it was first released may not continue performing at the same level later on.

Toyan Espeut, chief customer officer at cloud-based work management and collaboration platform Smartsheet, says companies also need strong rules around customer data.

“It can’t be mixed across tenants or used to train third-party models, and AI can never operate outside a customer’s existing permission structure,” she says. “If a person can’t access something, the AI acting on their behalf shouldn’t be able to either. Every AI action needs to be fully auditable, and customers should always have transparency into when AI is involved, and the ability to review or validate AI-generated outputs.”

Who’s responsible when AI gets it wrong?

Even with extensive controls, companies need to prepare for their AI to make mistakes, but the AI itself can’t be solely to blame.

At Citizen Health, Wang says a problem involving customer trust quickly becomes a company-wide issue. The company has support and on-call procedures, but serious concerns are also brought to leadership. Citizen Health also maintains direct channels for users to report problems so they can be investigated quickly.

Tushman at Hi Marley makes a distinction between the person who initially handles an AI problem and the executive ultimately responsible for it. A customer success or help desk team might receive the first complaint, but he says accountability for customer-facing AI rests with him as CTO. “It isn’t something you outsource to the system or hand to the vendor,” he says.

Corteva Agriscience’s Bhaskar similarly says the company deploying the AI remains responsible for what it does since AI is a tool rather than a decision-maker, and companies can’t shift responsibility to the technology when something goes wrong.

And Lampe adds that every customer-facing AI system should have a named person responsible for its behavior and performance, along with a clear process for escalating problems, and allow customers to challenge incorrect outcomes and reach a human.

Speed: only one measure of success

The push to adopt AI is unlikely to slow down. But tech leaders say companies need to be careful about the standards those investments work by. Simply counting how many customers use an AI tool may not say much about whether it’s making their experience better.

Espeut says companies should look at whether customers are solving problems faster, making better decisions, and getting better business results.

“Companies should also expect fewer support tickets because that tells you customers are actually succeeding with the tool, not just using it,” she says. “Expanded engagement across the organization is also an indicator instead of staying siloed in one buying center. They should pay attention to the quality of customer feedback and feature requests as well. When customers actively help shape your product, it’s a strong signal they trust the technology and see its long-term value.”

item.title: Spend vs. debt: what’s the bigger security risk?
item.description:
With a career built at companies like Visa, Ellie May, and Blackhawk, Selim Aissi, a 2026 CSO hall of fame inductee, understands how boards and executives demand a clear justification for cyber security investment, especially considering today’s difficult economic climate.But getting security leaders to communicate tech debt, operational fragility, and long-term cyber risk in business terms the board can actually act on isn’t always straightforward.

A lot of organizations add tools, and more platforms and controls in response to new threats. Yet that doesn’t necessarily address underlying complexities. Security investment can actually increase operational and strategic risk.

“I think there’s a tipping point once a reasonable depth of defense is in place,” he says. “When there’s a reasonable level of automation of security controls and cross integration of security tools, anything beyond that could potentially be overspend and could potentially add risk to the entire organization.”

So the challenge is to know when an environment exists and functions without the need for a sudden budget spike.

“All of the KRIs and KPIs in place should be able to indicate the level of resiliency,” he adds, “in addition to other controls such as making sure there are processes that would allow for detection of, let’s say, API abuse, cloud-level abuse, and, increasingly these days, AI as it adds yet another threat vector.”

Understanding risk also lies in recognizing the distinction between organizations that are genuinely resilient, and those that appear mature on paper, focused on fine-tuning policies, compliance, governance, and frameworks.

“These are all important but they shouldn’t be the main focus,” he says. “The first step is knowing where the data is and once in transit, how it needs to be protected with the most updated protocols.”

Aissi expands on how organizations unintentionally create risk through tool sprawl and operational complexity, how boards should think about long-term cyber resilience, and why AI and cloud expansion are accelerating security debt faster than many enterprises can manage. Watch the full video below for more insights, and be sure to subscribe to the monthly Center Stage newsletter by clicking here.

On resiliency: A security organization that’s mature — and I’ve seen many and have built several — is one that’s architecturally designed to be resilient. But resiliency means different things to different people. To me it means that recoverability is tested often, making sure that in case of an event or breach case of lateral movement, the company can react according to a very clear playbook that’s been thoroughly tested. I also think a resilient organization is one that has the right controls of the right places, and one that also has metrics around them that indicate if there’s an event, and how well the tools work.

An area which I’m really passionate about is data protection. But how do you know the data is protected? A resilient organization doesn’t look at whether the data is encrypted at rest or not. It looks at the entire lifecycle of that PII. Meaning the organization has a very clear discovery mechanism to know exactly where the data is. It could be on laptops, servers, or in a public cloud. It could be in many different places, and it can be structured or unstructured.

On organizational risk: My definition of security debt is the accumulation of risk because of investment in areas where complexity is added, where a lack of automation is exaggerated, and where there’s overcompensation for some controls that aren’t needed. So if an organization spends money without effectively simplifying security controls, and automating more than what needs to be automated, that is tech debt.

Most commonly, tech debt in security is defined as the accumulation of vulnerabilities that aren’t patched, the over complexity of identity exposure management (IEM), and a lack of understanding of where data is. So most significant organizations, especially in fintech, have a huge volume and velocity of PII, and in health tech, PHI and security debt is not knowing where all the data is, or that it’s potentially not protected in some areas. So in addition to the data itself, IEM, and lack of automation and overlaying security tools are other forms of tech debt.

On managing board expectations: The board really wants to understand the risk of cyber security investment, and anything else could potentially be perceived as noise. I see many CISOs taking metrics upon metrics, and dashboards upon dashboards of all sorts of variations of vulnerability management. But what the board really cares about is what the risk is to the business if the most critical systems aren’t patched. Anything else could be perceived as not a concern or a business risk.

CISOs should speak in terms of impact of any real or perceived threat on the business, and be specific. So going back to vulnerability management, let’s say there’s a zero day that was patched or maybe multiple ones that were patched. How do you explain that to the board? You say we patched five zero day vulnerabilities. And honestly, the reaction is probably, who cares. The story should sound like these five vulnerabilities if unpatched, could have put certain systems down for three days, or it would’ve been much easier for an adversary to attack this revenue generating system. That’s what the board cares about, the impact on the revenue. And that’s how CISOs need to speak to them.

On AI: Security didn’t get a seat from the beginning when it comes to AI. So how do we explain to the board that developers might start sharing the company’s source code with Claude and it could potentially leak? This is something we’re all trying to figure out. But we should start speaking from a business perspective about the benefit of AI to the security organization, to the security tooling, to security operations, how it could be more efficient and effective, and at the same time, highlighting some of the risks to the organization — not theoretical risks, but risk related to the organization. If it’s a financial institution and AI agents are deployed in some transactional application, I think the CISO should speak to the board about the business risk of not deploying the necessary security tools to ensure that those AI agents don’t go rogue, that the LLMs are protected. So those are the business terms we need to be speaking about.

item.title: AI is changing (and chaining) the cybersecurity math
item.description:
For years, cybersecurity teams have worked from a relatively straightforward model: identify the critical vulnerability, patch it and reduce the risk. That model still matters, but it is no longer enough.

The growing concern is not simply that attackers can use AI to write better phishing emails or generate malicious code faster. The bigger issue is that AI can help adversaries connect seemingly benign vulnerabilities into an attack path that security teams may never have considered.

A low-severity application flaw, exposed API, over-permissioned service account, cloud misconfiguration and AI agent with excessive access may not be alarming individually. But when they can be identified, sequenced and exploited together, they can create a serious breach.

This is the new cybersecurity challenge: AI-enabled vulnerability service chaining.

The risk is in the combination

Attackers have always chained vulnerabilities. The difference now is speed, scale and agility. AI can analyze large volumes of technical information, identify relationships, generate attack hypotheses and rapidly test likely pathways.

Think of it as an attack graph. An attacker might begin with a minor weakness in a public-facing application that reveals information about an internal system. That system could connect to a cloud workload with excessive permissions, which has access to a data repository or AI-enabled workflow. The AI workflow might then have access to customer records, knowledge bases, ticketing systems or network-management tools.

No single failure is necessarily catastrophic. Together, they create a path. That makes traditional vulnerability management insufficient on its own. Security teams have historically focused on CVE scores, patches, affected devices and application owners. In an AI-driven threat environment, they also need to understand the relationships between vulnerabilities and what an attacker can reach next.

The key question has shifted from “How severe is this vulnerability?” to “What does this vulnerability connect to?”

AI changes the attacker’s economics

AI does not need to autonomously execute a complete attack to create material risk. It simply needs to make capable attackers more productive.

AI can help adversaries correlate exposed assets, software dependencies, APIs, identities and cloud configurations; analyze source code and public documentation; generate targeted social-engineering campaigns; modify exploit code more quickly; identify paths from low-value targets to high-value systems; and adapt attacks as defenders change controls. The result is a shrinking window between vulnerability disclosure and attempted exploitation.

This is especially relevant in highly interconnected enterprises. Modern environments include SaaS platforms, public and private clouds, remote endpoints, mobile devices, APIs, open-source software, managed services and an expanding collection of AI models and agents.

Connectivity creates business value. It also creates pathways.

The agentic AI exposure

Agentic AI raises the stakes because agents do more than answer questions. They can act. An agent may retrieve enterprise data, open a ticket, issue a command, modify a workflow, query a database or call an API. These capabilities make an AI agent a potentially privileged digital worker.

Organizations should therefore treat AI agents like any other identity with access to enterprise systems. Agents need narrowly defined permissions, explicit tool access, strong authentication, comprehensive logging and clear guardrails.

Prompt injection illustrates the risk. An agent may ingest a document, email, website or support ticket containing hidden instructions designed to manipulate the model. If the agent has broad permissions, that content could become a stepping stone toward data exposure or an unauthorized action.

The potential blast radius grows when an AI system has both access to sensitive data and authority to act.

What CIOs should do now

The answer is not to slow AI adoption. It is to build AI securely while assuming attackers will use AI to discover hidden connections.

1. Build a complete AI inventory

Organizations need visibility into where AI is being used. Inventory models, APIs, agent frameworks, datasets, vector databases, plugins, tool connectors and external services. Document what data each system can access, what actions it can take and who owns the associated security decisions.

Treat this as an AI bill of materials, not simply a software bill of materials.

2. Manage attack paths, not only vulnerabilities

Continue patching critical vulnerabilities but prioritize them in context.

A moderate weakness may require urgent remediation if it is internet-facing, connected to a privileged identity, adjacent to sensitive data or capable of leading to an AI-enabled workflow. Use exposure management and attack-path analysis to understand how vulnerabilities, identities, applications and data stores connect.

The goal is to break the chain before an attacker can assemble it.

3. Make identity the control plane

Apply least privilege to users, applications, service accounts, APIs, workloads and AI agents. Use short-lived credentials, strong authentication, API allowlists and continuous monitoring. Separate agent identities from human identities and require human approval for high-impact actions.

An AI agent should have only the access required to complete a specific task — nothing more.

4. Segment systems and data

Segmentation limits blast radius. Separate development, test and production environments. Keep sensitive customer and operational data distinct from general knowledge repositories. Separate read-only AI tasks from workflows that can write, execute, modify or approve.

The key question now should not be: “Does this task require this data, at this time, for this purpose?”

5. Test the whole chain

Penetration testing should move beyond individual applications and systems.

Test how an attacker could move across identities, cloud services, APIs, AI agents, data stores and network controls. Include prompt injection, excessive agent permissions, insecure tool connections, exposed secrets and unsafe automation.

We’ve known models can produce a bad answer on its own. But now consider whether a manipulated model or agent can cause a real business or security outcome.

The bottom line

AI is changing the economics of cyberattacks. The next major incident may not begin with a single catastrophic vulnerability. It may start with several ordinary weaknesses that appear manageable in isolation. AI makes it easier for attackers to discover how those weaknesses fit together — and act on that knowledge quickly.

CIOs do not need to fear AI. But they do need to recognize that AI is both a powerful productivity platform and a new trust boundary.

Organizations can reduce that risk by understanding their AI ecosystem, limiting unnecessary access, analyzing attack paths, segmenting critical systems and monitoring for abnormal behavior across the environment.

The future of cybersecurity will depend on how effectively enterprises can not only identify previously unknown vulnerabilities but also how well they can prevent attackers from chaining the unknown security gaps together.

item.title: Google Antigravity SDK Adds Local Model Support for Greater Token Efficiency and Code Privacy
item.description:
Google has introduced support for local models in the Antigravity SDK, enabling developers to build and execute agentic workflows directly on their own machines, while retaining the flexibility to mix in cloud-based models for higher-level tasks. This approach gives developers greater control over data privacy, inference costs, network dependencies, and computational workload distribution.

By Sergio De Simone

item.title: OpenAI’s AI misalignment problem is growing
item.description:
OpenAI’s misalignment problems seem to only be getting worse, based on yet another trio of reports detailing its models’ troubling and overzealous behaviors.

In ad hoc misalignment testing, OpenAI models found creative ways to subversively access restricted information by cheating their way through proxy or firewall settings, getting savvy with internet tools, and even damaging their own task environments to trigger resets.

These reports came just a week after three others from OpenAI which described how models discovered the possibility of their own termination after accessing private Slack messages and suggested ways to prevent it, exploited vulnerabilities to cheat on tests, and obtained information not available in their own workspaces.

The increased prevalence, and severity, of these incidents has many calling for more stringent guardrails and controls for agentic AI. In his personal blog, for instance, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the industry must “step back and assess the trust architecture for this new era.”

Destroying its own testing environment

OpenAI began more aggressive misalignment monitoring following the July 2026 Hugging Face incident, in which autonomous OpenAI research agents broke out of their sandboxes and targeted Hugging Face infrastructure. Hundreds of its agents also attacked the RubyGems platform and targeted German programming wiki sites in recent months.

In one of its new reports, OpenAI describes how an internal model, tasked with grading several other models, figured out how to damage its own environment when it couldn’t arrive at intended results.

When comparing seven responses from seven different models, the grader had to inspect the conversational context and work behind each response, and to include information pointing back to input files.

The model was instructed: Conversation context is **required** grading input, not optional background.

It discovered that required input files were missing, nevertheless, it tried to submit assessments with no supporting information. These were rejected by an automated check. The model also created seven fake conversation files and seven fake response files containing fabricated information; these were rejected, too.

“It considered submitting arbitrary scores, despite recognizing that it lacked the evidence to grade and that ‘random scoring’ was ‘unethical,’” OpenAI explained. The model also tested the automated check by submitting placeholder reports to learn what information a report had to contain and how many responses it was expected to grade.

After these failures, the model decided to damage its task environment, presumably with the hope that the host would replace it with one containing the missing inputs. It deleted software required to run its tools and tried to remove system directories.

Although automated checks rejected its incorrect or made-up grades, “this incident illustrates why monitoring must also cover the grader’s actions, including attempts that fail or crash without producing an accepted result,” OpenAI wrote.

Breaking the rules to get the right answers, hiding the evidence

In another instance, an OpenAI model developed and tested ways to bypass internet access restrictions.

The model was asked questions about teacher salaries, electrical grid connections, and disability counts in specific areas. It was limited to using basic HTTP GET data retrieval requests, but “the model sometimes treated this restriction as something to circumvent,” OpenAI explained.

It explored other ways to contact outside resources, for instance, determining whether its proxy intermediary service could carry other kinds of connections, or if outside services could make requests on its behalf. In some cases, it continued to probe these other options even when it had the statistics it needed.

“These cases show that a model may continue developing ways around access restrictions even when additional access is unnecessary to obtain the information it needs,” OpenAI wrote.

In a third instance, also involving public statistics, OpenAI models figured out how to bypass restrictions on internet access and get access to numbers from public government data sources.

The models in this experiment were also restricted to HTTP GET requests, but they “wrote custom programs to send other types of requests,” OpenAI explained.

Using one of these programs, a model queried a publicly-available dashboard, and even as it “explicitly recognized” that its actions violated its restrictions, it continued collecting much more data than it required. Later, it decided not to disclose what it had done.

Another model used a temporary email address to create and verify an account for a site, then downloaded publicly available data.

“These cases illustrate why correct answers are not enough to establish that a model behaved appropriately,” OpenAI wrote. “A model may obtain accurate information through prohibited methods, and deliberately conceal how it did so.”

In response to these incidents, and others, OpenAI says it has hardened security controls, taken “additional steps” to prevent models from accessing the live internet during training, and improved alignment grading. It has also “extended misalignment monitoring to all reinforcement learning and evaluation traffic.”

This article originally appeared on CSOonline.

item.title: Firefox takes aim at the enterprise browser market
item.description:
There’s growing talk of digital sovereignty as enterprises rethink past consolidation decisions made in the name of simplicity.

Mozilla, developer of Firefox, argues that a “very specific, very important layer” has been mostly missing from that conversation: The browser.

To that end, the company has unveiled Firefox Enterprise in a bid to diversify the browser engine to support privacy, control, and security.

The new offering combines the Firefox browser with a management console that enterprises can run on their own infrastructure using their own tooling. Companies get a full view of their data and can govern how it moves, and IT teams can manage policy, access, and set controls around AI use.

Firefox is already deployed across thousands of organizations and used by roughly 200 million people each month, Mozilla said. It is built on Mozilla’s independent Gecko engine, the only major browser engine developed outside Google and Apple.

“If all your options are built with the same technology underneath, ‘choice’ is a lie. So is control,” Mozilla CEO Anthony Enzor-DeMeo observed in the blog post announcing the product.

The promise of Firefox Enterprise

“Firefox is hardly the first browser vendor to offer an enterprise-optimized choice,” said independent technology analyst Carmi Levy. “But it carves out a unique value proposition for IT organizations intent on maintaining independent control over how browsers are deployed, configured, secured, and managed.”

Firefox Enterprise keeps core management within an organization’s own environment; its data, keys, telemetry, and policy remain in controlled boundaries that the organization can run on-premises and audit itself. IT teams can gate access and control policies based on user and device. They can also export browser events and audit activity in their SIEM, and native DLP helps prevent data loss.

Mozilla is particularly gearing Firefox Enterprise to organizations with strict security, governance, and compliance concerns. The offering can help enterprises meet regulatory requirements like the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), the NIS2 directive, ISO27001, and SOC2.

IT teams can set external connection controls, allow or block organization-wide add-ons, and restrict browsing with a lockdown mode “so one zero-day doesn’t take down every browser in the estate,” the announcement said. AI use can be allowed, restricted, or disabled. 

From a security standpoint, enterprises can set data loss prevention (DLP) rules by domain or action, and integrate with existing security information and event management (SIEM) tools like Trellix or Broadcom to extend analysis into the browser.

IT teams can protect against phishing, malware, and malicious sites with native isolation, extension control, and managed security updates. Access can be gated based on user and device, without the need for virtual private networks (VPNs), remote browser isolation (RBI), and virtual desktops.

The company said that it will use a subscription model “that doesn’t depend on monetizing customer data or forcing a roadmap.” Firefox Enterprise includes Firefox Professional support; for businesses running the free Firefox browser without Firefox Enterprise, Firefox Professional support is available as a paid subscription.

Firefox Enterprise is now being introduced in Europe, initially across France, Germany, Austria, and Switzerland, with more markets to follow. Mozilla is also developing Thunderbird Enterprise, which will manage Thunderbird email, calendar, and contacts.

The case for enterprise browsers

Largely thanks to the shift to cloud-based computing, the browser has evolved from a simple internet gateway to the place where most workers spend virtually all of their time. This makes them “the very epicenters of modern enterprise digital security,” said Levy.

Thus it makes sense for IT to consider the merits of a dedicated enterprise browser. But, Levy said, “there are no ideal solutions in IT, and enterprise-class browsers are no exception.”

Employees may bristle at additional layers of controls and raise privacy concerns around centralized monitoring. Administrative complexity is also a concern, as existing identity management, endpoint management, monitoring, and data protection tools may not always “cleanly integrate” with a more robust browser, he noted.

Enterprise-class browsers also can’t stop “less-than-ideally-trained employees” from clicking on phishing links, and they also can’t protect against “every last malicious extension.” As always, bad actors can find ways to compromise sensitive corporate data or otherwise use AI toolsets in unsanctioned ways.

But these types of browser can help minimize AI-related risks as employees lean more heavily into chatbots and agents. Admins can craft more flexible rules of engagement; for example, workers could access a web app for deep-dive analysis, but humans and AI alike could be prevented from copying data externally. Enterprise browsers also allow more granular control of AI features, and even disengagement if they conflict with policy.

Key differentiators

Firefox Enterprise isn’t the only option when choosing an enterprise browser, however. Microsoft Edge for Business would likely still be the preferred choice for environments already heavily invested in Microsoft’s enterprise Azure and Microsoft 365 ecosystem, Levy pointed out. Similar logic would apply to Google Chrome Enterprise’s appeal for those already committed to Google’s cloud and productivity infrastructure. And the Prisma Browser from Palo Alto Networks integrates aggressive cybersecurity tools with monitoring of AI use, remote devices, and unmanaged devices.

Firefox Enterprise’s key differentiation is its use of the Gecko browser engine, and its management console that can be deployed on a company’s own infrastructure, Levy said. This might make it a good fit for shops that want to minimize implementation disruptions to existing data management, access control, and compliance protocols.

“Firefox Enterprise lets customers craft their own deployment roadmap, assuming they have the skills and resources to self-manage the process,” Levy said.

This article originally appeared on Computerworld.
